441.quote_or_event: “How is the Society of the Saints to be known? There, the Name of the One Lord is chanted.”
441.explanation: Guru Nanak gives a test for recognising true company (satsangat): it is the gathering where the One Name is praised.
441.tie_back: The Kural tells one to learn the right way, weigh carefully, and then win the friendship of the wise; Guru Nanak likewise gives a criterion for discerning which company is truly worth joining.
441.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 72, Siree Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
441._accuracy_note: A strong fit on discerning and seeking worthy company; the Kural's 'great men' are counsellors mature in dharma and knowledge, while Gurbani's test is devotion to the Naam.

442.quote_or_event: “In the Company of the Holy, the five passions are brought to rest.”
442.explanation: In the Sukhmani Guru Arjan lists the benefits of the Saadh Sangat, including bringing the five vices under control.
442.tie_back: The Kural values those who remove troubles that have come and guard against troubles to come; Guru Arjan presents holy company as the force that subdues the inner afflictions behind them.
442.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 271, Raag Gauree (Sukhmani), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
442._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: the Kural speaks of advisers who cure and prevent all kinds of trouble, including political ones, while the Sukhmani speaks of inner vices only.

443.quote_or_event: “They alone are relatives, and they alone are friends, who, as Gurmukh, join together in love.”
443.explanation: Guru Amar Das redefines kinship: one's true relatives and friends are those who live as Gurmukhs, turned towards the Guru, and meet in love.
443.tie_back: The Kural calls it the rarest of rare things to honour the great and make them one's own kin; Guru Amar Das likewise counts the God-oriented as one's real family.
443.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 643, Raag Sorath, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
443._accuracy_note: A strong fit on making the worthy one's kin; the line does not stress rarity, and its 'great' are Gurmukhs rather than wise counsellors of state.

444.quote_or_event: Lehna, while on a pilgrimage to a Hindu goddess's shrine, met Guru Nanak and resolved to follow him; known for his loyalty to the first Guru, he became Nanak's successor as Guru Angad.
444.explanation: Lehna placed himself under one greater than himself and served him with such devotion that Guru Nanak chose him as the second Guru.
444.tie_back: The Kural calls it the foremost strength to conduct oneself so that those greater than oneself become one's own; Lehna's loyal discipleship made the greatest teacher of his age wholly his own.
444._accuracy_note: A strong illustrative parallel from well-attested Sikh history; Britannica gives the outline, and fuller accounts of Lehna's service come from later tradition.

445.quote_or_event: “The Guru has applied the true ointment of spiritual wisdom to my eyes.”
445.explanation: Guru Amar Das describes the Guru as the one who gives true sight, anointing the eyes with spiritual wisdom (gian anjan).
445.tie_back: The Kural says a king sees through his counsellors as his eyes and must choose them carefully; in Gurbani the Guru is the one who gives the eyes true vision.
445.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 124, Raag Maajh, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
445._accuracy_note: The 'counsel as eyes' image matches well, but the Sikh Guru is a spiritual guide given by grace, not a minister chosen by a ruler's deliberation.

446.quote_or_event: “In the Company of the Holy, all one's enemies become friends.”
446.explanation: In the Sukhmani Guru Arjan teaches that within the Saadh Sangat enmity dissolves and even former enemies become friends.
446.tie_back: The Kural says enemies can do nothing to one who lives in the fellowship of the worthy; Guru Arjan says that in such fellowship enmity itself disappears.
446.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 271, Raag Gauree (Sukhmani), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
446._accuracy_note: A strong fit: both make the company of the good a protection against enemies; the Kural means enemies are powerless, Gurbani that enmity is transformed.

447.quote_or_event: “If my heart is pure, and I am slandered, then the slanderer washes my clothes.” … “One who slanders me is my friend.”
447.explanation: Bhagat Kabir welcomes those who expose his faults, saying such critics cleanse him and are really his friends.
447.tie_back: The Kural asks who can ruin one who keeps companions able to rebuke him; Kabir likewise treats the one who points out his faults as a friend who keeps him clean.
447.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 339, Raag Gauree, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
447._accuracy_note: Strong on welcoming correction as friendship; Kabir speaks of hostile slanderers, whereas the Kural means trusted counsellors who rebuke out of loyalty.

448.quote_or_event: “One who is attached to Maya is totally blind and deaf. He does not listen to the Word of the Shabad; he makes a great uproar and tumult.”
448.explanation: Guru Amar Das describes the person ruled by Maya as deaf to the Guru's corrective Word, lost in his own noise.
448.tie_back: The Kural says the king with no one to rebuke him perishes even without enemies; Guru Amar Das portrays the one who will not hear correction as destroying himself from within.
448.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 313, Raag Gauree (Gauree ki Vaar, salok), Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
448._accuracy_note: Next-best only: the line shares the idea of refusing correction, but it does not state the Kural's point that such a person is ruined without any external enemy.

449.quote_or_event: “O Nanak, without capital, no one has ever departed with profit.”
449.explanation: Guru Nanak uses the language of trade: without the capital of spiritual wisdom and virtue, no one leaves this world with any gain.
449.tie_back: The Kural says there is no profit without capital and no stability without the support of the worthy; Guru Nanak uses the same capital-and-profit image for the spiritual life.
449.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1244, Raag Saarang (Saarang ki Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
449._accuracy_note: The capital-and-profit metaphor matches closely, but in Gurbani the capital is spiritual wisdom (commentators gloss it as gian or faith), not the backing of great men.

450.quote_or_event: During the siege of Anandpur in 1705, some Sikhs signed a disclaimer (bedava) disowning Guru Gobind Singh and left; shamed at home and led back by Mai Bhago, they rejoined the Guru and fell fighting at Khidrana (Muktsar), where the Guru tore up the bedava at the dying Mahan Singh's request.
450.explanation: Abandoning the Guru's company proved a far deeper loss to these Sikhs than the danger they fled, and they won back honour only by returning to it at the cost of their lives.
450.tie_back: The Kural says giving up the friendship of the good is ten times worse than the enmity of many; the deserters found leaving the Guru worse than facing the besieging armies.
450.source: Encyclopaedia of Sikhism (ed. Harbans Singh, Punjabi University), 'Bedava', as published on thesikhencyclopedia.com (paraphrase)
450._accuracy_note: A strong narrative parallel from Sikh tradition (based on later sources such as Gurbilas and Suraj Granth); details such as the torn bedava come from tradition, and the Kural's 'ten times' calculus is not explicit.
